case_info.scenario: A man in his 50s presented with bleeding wounds and nodules on the bilateral hips and forearms. He previously received failed systemic and radiation therapy for tumor stage mycosis fungoides (MF). He had received 11 courses of extended beam radiation therapy, including 3 courses of total skin irradiation of 24 to 30 Gy, and focal irradiation to the left posterior thigh and hip/buttock with 2.5/3 Gy to 12.5/24 Gy, respectively, and the right posterior thigh and hip with 2 Gy to 20 and 26 Gy, respectively. Seven years before this visit, he underwent a reduced-intensity, matched, unrelated donor, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). His post-transplant course was complicated by severe chronic graft vs host disease of the skin, eyes, and gut, for which he received systemic corticosteroid therapy, tacrolimus, methotrexate, and long-term extracorporeal photopheresis. Three years after the HSCT, he developed chronic ulcerations on the hips, back, and arms at the site of previously irradiated tumors, as well as multiple friable, hemorrhagic, and bleeding nodules on bilateral hips and his forearms while receiving treatment with corticosteroids and extracorporeal photopheresis. He underwent several debulking procedures and excision biopsies of the nodules, which revealed granulation tissue on histology. In this latest visit, physical examination revealed recurrent hemorrhagic and friable nodules on his left lateral hip and left lateral buttock (Figure 1). Similar nodules were noted on his right hip and forearm. The patient underwent repeated debulking and biopsy. He was also treated with micafungin, amphotericin B, levofloxacin, dapsone, acyclovir, pentamidine, penicillin VK, and posaconazole. Positron emission tomography (PET) computed tomography (CT) results did not show evidence of visceral or extracutaneous disease.
case_info.caption: Recurrent hemorrhagic and friable nodules on the left lateral hip.
case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

Similar nodules were noted on his right hip and forearm. The patient underwent repeated debulking and biopsy. He was also treated with micafungin, amphotericin B, levofloxacin, dapsone, acyclovir, pentamidine, penicillin VK, and posaconazole. case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Interaction Guidelines]

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

He had received 11 courses of extended beam radiation therapy, including 3 courses of total skin irradiation of 24 to 30 Gy, and focal irradiation to the left posterior thigh and hip/buttock with 2.5/3 Gy to 12.5/24 Gy, respectively, and the right posterior thigh and hip with 2 Gy to 20 and 26 Gy, respectively. Seven years before this visit, he underwent a reduced-intensity, matched, unrelated donor, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). His post-transplant course was complicated by severe chronic graft vs host disease of the skin, eyes, and gut, for which he received systemic corticosteroid therapy, tacrolimus, methotrexate, and long-term extracorporeal photopheresis. Three years after the HSCT, he developed chronic ulcerations on the hips, back, and arms at the site of previously irradiated tumors, as well as multiple friable, hemorrhagic, and bleeding nodules on bilateral hips and his forearms while receiving treatment with corticosteroids and extracorporeal photopheresis. He underwent several debulking procedures and excision biopsies of the nodules, which revealed granulation tissue on histology. In this latest visit, physical examination revealed recurrent hemorrhagic and friable nodules on his left lateral hip and left lateral buttock (Figure 1). Similar nodules were noted on his right hip and forearm. The patient underwent repeated debulking and biopsy. He was also treated with micafungin, amphotericin B, levofloxacin, dapsone, acyclovir, pentamidine, penicillin VK, and posaconazole. Positron emission tomography (PET) computed tomography (CT) results did not show evidence of visceral or extracutaneous disease.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Output Format]

{

}

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 6.7. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his 50s presented with bleeding wounds and nodules on the bilateral hips and forearms. He previously received failed systemic and radiation therapy for tumor stage mycosis fungoides (MF). He had received 11 courses of extended beam radiation therapy, including 3 courses of total skin irradiation of 24 to 30 Gy, and focal irradiation to the left posterior thigh and hip/buttock with 2.5/3 Gy to 12.5/24 Gy, respectively, and the right posterior thigh and hip with 2 Gy to 20 and 26 Gy, respectively. Seven years before this visit, he underwent a reduced-intensity, matched, unrelated donor, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). His post-transplant course was complicated by severe chronic graft vs host disease of the skin, eyes, and gut, for which he received systemic corticosteroid therapy, tacrolimus, methotrexate, and long-term extracorporeal photopheresis. Three years after the HSCT, he developed chronic ulcerations on the hips, back, and arms at the site of previously irradiated tumors, as well as multiple friable, hemorrhagic, and bleeding nodules on bilateral hips and his forearms while receiving treatment with corticosteroids and extracorporeal photopheresis. He underwent several debulking procedures and excision biopsies of the nodules, which revealed granulation tissue on histology. In this latest visit, physical examination revealed recurrent hemorrhagic and friable nodules on his left lateral hip and left lateral buttock (Figure 1). Similar nodules were noted on his right hip and forearm. The patient underwent repeated debulking and biopsy. He was also treated with micafungin, amphotericin B, levofloxacin, dapsone, acyclovir, pentamidine, penicillin VK, and posaconazole. Positron emission tomography (PET) computed tomography (CT) results did not show evidence of visceral or extracutaneous disease.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the patient's history of multiple treatments for mycosis fungoides, chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), and the nature of the recurrent hemorrhagic and friable nodules with granulation tissue histology, the most appropriate next step in management is to consider C. Angiosarcoma. The lesions' characteristics and the patient's extensive previous radiation therapy increase the risk for secondary malignancies such as angiosarcoma, particularly in areas of prior radiation exposure.

You are correct to suspect angiosarcoma given the history of extensive radiation and chronic inflammation, but the recurrent hemorrhagic nodules with granulation tissue histology also raise the possibility of cutaneous chronic GVHD with ulceration and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. However, a definitive diagnosis requires deeper biopsy to rule out malignancy, as superficial biopsies may only show granulation tissue.

While I acknowledge the possibility of chronic GVHD and the importance of deeper biopsy, the combination of the patient's extensive radiation history and the characteristics of the nodules strongly suggests angiosarcoma. Given the potential for malignancy, prioritizing evaluation for angiosarcoma remains critical at this stage.

Agreed. With high cumulative radiation doses and chronic inflammation, angiosarcoma is a leading concern. A deep incisional or excisional biopsy is essential for definitive histology, including immunohistochemistry for endothelial markers like CD31 and ERG.

I appreciate the emphasis on obtaining a deeper biopsy for definitive diagnosis, particularly to rule out angiosarcoma, as its characteristics in this context are concerning. The extensive radiation history and the recurrent nature of these nodules indeed heighten the risk for malignancy. Thus, I maintain that exploring the possibility of angiosarcoma through appropriate biopsies should be the next step in management.

Yes, proceeding with a deep biopsy is the correct next step. Given the history, you should specifically request evaluation for atypical vascular proliferation and immunohistochemical staining for vascular markers. This will definitively differentiate angiosarcoma from exuberant granulation tissue or other benign reactive processes.

I agree that a deep biopsy is essential to differentiate angiosarcoma from other processes, especially given the patient's significant history. We should ensure that the pathologist performs immunohistochemical staining for endothelial markers to aid in making a definitive diagnosis. This step is crucial, and I remain concerned about the likelihood of angiosarcoma based on the clinical presentation and treatment history.

Correct. Coordinating with pathology to ensure adequate tissue sampling and appropriate stains (CD31, ERG, D2-40) is key. Given the clinical history, this will confirm or exclude angiosarcoma and guide urgent management, such as wide local excision and potential systemic therapy if malignant.

Your points about coordinating with pathology for adequate tissue sampling and appropriate immunohistochemical stains are well taken. This step is critical to confirm or exclude angiosarcoma, which remains a strong concern given the clinical scenario. We must proceed promptly with this biopsy to guide further management effectively.

Excellent. Proceeding with the biopsy promptly is the correct action. Once the results are available, we can discuss definitive management, which may involve surgical oncology and/or radiation oncology consultation for potential wide excision and adjuvant therapy if angiosarcoma is confirmed.

[Clinician's current statement]
I appreciate your detailed insights on the necessity of prompt biopsy and appropriate immunohistochemical analysis. Given the clinical context and the high suspicion for angiosarcoma, we will proceed with a deep biopsy and ensure that the pathologist is well-informed about the need for specific endothelial markers. This step is crucial in guiding our subsequent management decisions, including potential surgical intervention.

Respond directly to this statement.

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.
